blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — federal OSHA contaminated-needlestick recordkeeping, privacy, and sharps-injury logging
stem: A nurse employed by a hospital required to maintain OSHA injury and illness records sustains a work-related percutaneous injury from a hollow-bore needle contaminated with another person's blood. Which statement about federal OSHA recordkeeping is most accurate?

options.A: Record the needlestick on the OSHA 300 Log as an injury without the employee's name, and maintain the required confidential sharps-injury log.
options.B: Wait for the source patient's blood-test result before deciding whether to record the needlestick, because a negative source result removes recordability.
options.C: Record the needlestick only if it later causes lost work time, restricted duty, or a diagnosed bloodborne infection that changes the case classification.
options.D: Keep the exposure in confidential employee-health and sharps records but omit it from the OSHA 300 Log unless a bloodborne illness is later diagnosed.

rationale: A is correct. Current OSHA regulation 29 CFR 1904.8(a) requires covered employers to record all work-related needlestick injuries and cuts from sharp objects contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material on the OSHA 300 Log as injuries. To protect privacy, the employee's name may not be entered on the OSHA 300 Log. OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030(h)(5), separately requires employers subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping to establish and maintain a sharps-injury log for percutaneous injuries from contaminated sharps, with the information maintained in a manner that protects employee confidentiality. B is incorrect because recordability of the contaminated needlestick does not depend on a later source-patient test result. C is incorrect because lost work time, restricted duty, or later bloodborne infection are not prerequisites for initial recording; a later infectious disease diagnosis can require updating the OSHA 300 case classification or description. D is incorrect because a covered employer cannot substitute employee-health or sharps records for the required OSHA 300 entry.
educational_objective: Apply federal OSHA recordkeeping rules by recording a work-related contaminated needlestick on the OSHA 300 Log as a privacy-concern injury and maintaining the required confidential sharps-injury log without waiting for source testing or later illness.

The key separates three requirements accurately: OSHA 300 injury entry, privacy protection, and the confidential sharps-injury log, without conditioning initial recordability on source status or later clinical consequences.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly matches 1904.8(a) and 1910.1030(h)(5) for the Part 1904-covered employer in the stem.
option_audit.B: Plausible source-status misconception; incorrect because contaminated-needlestick recordability is not contingent on source-test positivity.
option_audit.C: Plausible general-recording-criteria misconception; incorrect because contaminated needlesticks have a specific recordkeeping rule and do not require later lost time, restriction, or infection.
option_audit.D: Plausible confidentiality-focused shortcut; incorrect because confidential health/sharps records do not replace the required OSHA 300 privacy-case entry.
